lesson_title: One Proton, Two Definitions: The Real Meaning of Acid and Base
hook_text: Ammonia has no hydroxide in its formula — yet it's one of chemistry's classic bases. Here's the one-move explanation.
clip_script: Now the pass that catches everyone off guard. Ammonia enters water — and the THROWER this time is water. NH3 makes the catch, becoming NH4 plus, and the water molecule that gave up its proton walks away as hydroxide, OH minus. So ammonia earns its base badge not by carrying hydroxide — it owns none — but by being an excellent catcher. Better still, the catch itself manufactures hydroxide out of the robbed water. The old rulebook, which insisted a base must arrive with hydroxide in its kit bag, could never call that play; the pass-the-ball rulebook calls it instantly. Every question in this topic secretly asks one of two things: who threw, and who caught. Scan the equation for the species that lost an H from left to right — that was your thrower, the acid. Find the species that gained an H — your catcher, the base.
visual_style: Molecules drawn as players on a chalkboard pitch; a glowing proton arcs from a water molecule to ammonia; the emptied water molecule flashes and relabels itself OH minus; scoreboard flips ACID and BASE labels.
mood: Playful reveal — a famous puzzle collapsing into one obvious move.
pacing: Puzzle stated cold, beat of silence on the hydroxide-free formula, quick-cut pass animation, calm two-rule takeaway.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read any acid-base equation on sight.
